Simran (9) arrived after lunch and announced, "I'm bored," four times in the first twenty minutes. She lay on the floor, then on the sofa, then under the table. I didn't offer the tablet or a craft; I told her she could help me fold clothes or find her own thing. She groaned.

She had started "The Colony Times": a report on the new stray kitten, an interview with the watchman (she went down and asked him three questions), and a weather forecast: "Hot. Still hot."

Tuesday, at Nana's house

Diary, today was the BORINGEST day of the holidays. It rained all afternoon, the power went, and Nana was sleeping. No TV. No phone signal in the village. I said "I'm bored" to Nani so many times she started saying it back to me.
Kishore and I lay on the verandah looking at the rain for about a hundred years. Then I noticed the water running down the drain along the courtyard really fast. I tore a page from my old notebook and made a boat. Kishore made one too. We raced them from the tulsi pot to the gate. Then we made rules: a boat that sinks loses three points, a boat that gets stuck on a leaf can be poked once with a stick.
I won 14 to 11. Kishore says he wants a rematch tomorrow. I hope it rains.
Ujjwal

Preeti, you keep saying everything is boring and nothing matters. Your Vijay Nana knows that feeling. I was sixteen in 1979. I had a cricket bat, a transistor radio, friends at every corner of the mohalla. And one summer, none of it tasted of anything. I'd stand in the field at cricket thinking, why? I'd switch off the radio halfway through my favourite song. My mother thought I was ill. I wasn't sad, exactly. I was empty, like a bucket with a hole in it.
Then our headmaster asked a few of us to teach the small children of the construction workers in the evenings. Letters, counting. I went because I had nothing better to do. The first time a little girl read a word on her own, something moved in my chest. It wasn't fun, beta. It was more than fun. It mattered.
And if the empty feeling stays heavy, you tell your mother or me. We'll find help together.

Ritu Didi,

Kalyani

qa.q: What does Kalyani hear at night in the hostel?
qa.a: It is so quiet she can hear the clock.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani tell Shalini she had a cold?
qa.a: She was afraid of seeming childish, since everyone else seemed fine.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kalyani most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mrs Sen the same day; she reassured Kalyani and arranged an extra call home.

qa.q: How might Ritu Didi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She might feel a pang of missing her sister, and glad that Kalyani told Mrs Sen and asked for a Sunday call.

grounding: A teen at a residential school misses home food, sounds and routines at night and hides it from roommates.
